doc.title: Jay Leonhart interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: TV shows, jingles and the 1985 Mazola upright bass commercial
summary: He did TV and jingle work on electric bass; the 1985 Mazola commercial brought upright bass back into the mix, and he avoided Broadway pits.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: What kind of recording sessions would you have done on the electric bass? Was it T.V. shows?
T.V. shows and jingles. Lots of commercials. All those innocuous — Crest commercials and so forth and so on. A lot of them I did.
So at any moment you could hear yourself on the television?

Unfortunately, yes. Well actually you know it’s funny. On electric bass you didn’t hear yourself so well because they always put you down in the mix. So you say I think I played that commercial. I started playing — the first really big commercial I did on upright bass was a Mazola commercial: [sings] Mazola is the da, da, da, da. And I started really using upright bass in a four-four jazz situation. I remember the date. It was like 1985, in August 1985, and that commercial became a big hit and everybody said you know, upright bass is good. And so they started using it, and started bringing it way up in the mix, and suddenly you could hear yourself on all the commercials. And they wanted someone who could play real jazz, who really knew his way around the instrument, and they used me anyway.

Right no one else. So I got to be busier and busier, and I stayed around New York and people knew me, and so I just started making enough money in the commercials to hang around and play the jazz gigs at night, the occasional Broadway show, although I didn’t like that, I’m too much a ham to be in the pit. I like to be on the stage with people saying I’m here to hear that music, that music’s not to accompany that over there. So that’s sort of what I did. That’s why I’m here this weekend.
Well I can tell you’re a bit of a — you like to be on stage — I can tell by watching you.
